ground_truth_core_content:
Introduction:
**1:** Both sections argue that a single LLM call cannot handle complex problems the way a multi-step system can, and both preview the same four patterns. As in one of the other preset-5 articles, the generated section's version of this argument is thin and has no personal anecdote, but the core substantive contrast (isolated calls vs. robust architected systems) is present.

The Challenge with Complex Single LLM Calls:
**1:** Both sections argue single complex prompts are hard to debug, lack modularity, suffer from lost-in-the-middle, and are inefficient/unreliable as complexity grows, and both walk through the identical FAQ example. As in every article graded, the phrasing-sensitivity and context-overflow points have no clean standalone counterpart, treated as tolerable compression. Separately (not scored here -- see the note on this at the top level): this section's code consistently uses an old/incompatible Gemini SDK pattern (genai.GenerativeModel + tools=[PydanticClass] + response.candidates[0].content.parts[0].function_call + PydanticClass.from_dict(), none of which is how either the old or new google-genai SDK actually returns structured output) instead of the expected section's client.models.generate_content(..., config=types.GenerateContentConfig(response_schema=...)) pattern. The conceptual idea (Pydantic-validated structured output) is still present, so this is not counted as a CoreContent gap, but it is flagged prominently below as a new, more severe kind of issue than seen in prior articles.

The Power of Modularity: Why Chain LLM Calls?:
**1:** All four of the guideline's clearly-named benefits are present. This is one of the few articles graded where the expected section's distinct 'instructions may only make sense together and lose their meaning when split' point has an explicit, standalone counterpart ('some instructions may only make sense when presented together, losing their intended meaning when split across multiple prompts'), alongside the separate cost/latency and information-loss/'context drift' points. Only the 'glue code' maintenance-burden point remains unmatched, treated as tolerable compression.

Building a Sequential Workflow: FAQ Generation Pipeline:
**1:** Both sections build the identical 3-step chain, combine it into a sequential_workflow function, and measure a comparable execution time (~17-22s here vs. the expected section's 22.20s). Separately (not scored here -- see the note on this at the top level): this section's code consistently uses an old/incompatible Gemini SDK pattern (genai.GenerativeModel + tools=[PydanticClass] + response.candidates[0].content.parts[0].function_call + PydanticClass.from_dict(), none of which is how either the old or new google-genai SDK actually returns structured output) instead of the expected section's client.models.generate_content(..., config=types.GenerateContentConfig(response_schema=...)) pattern. The conceptual idea (Pydantic-validated structured output) is still present, so this is not counted as a CoreContent gap, but it is flagged prominently below as a new, more severe kind of issue than seen in prior articles.

Optimizing Sequential Workflows With Parallel Processing:
**1:** Both sections explain the independence of answering/sourcing, build the same async function pair and asyncio.gather-based parallel_workflow, report a comparable speedup (~2x here vs. the expected section's ~2.5x), cover the sequential-vs-parallel trade-off, and include a rate-limit caution (backoff with jitter). Separately (not scored here -- see the note on this at the top level): this section's code consistently uses an old/incompatible Gemini SDK pattern (genai.GenerativeModel + tools=[PydanticClass] + response.candidates[0].content.parts[0].function_call + PydanticClass.from_dict(), none of which is how either the old or new google-genai SDK actually returns structured output) instead of the expected section's client.models.generate_content(..., config=types.GenerateContentConfig(response_schema=...)) pattern. The conceptual idea (Pydantic-validated structured output) is still present, so this is not counted as a CoreContent gap, but it is flagged prominently below as a new, more severe kind of issue than seen in prior articles.

Introducing Dynamic Behavior: Routing and Conditional Logic:
**0:** The core ideas -- fixed workflows can't adapt, an LLM call as classifier, divide-and-conquer, and a customer-service illustration -- are all present, and the section adds well-sourced depth (a rule-engine alternative for small intent sets, compound-intent failure modes) and breadth (a decision-tree analogy) not in the expected section -- see DepthEnhancement/BreadthEnhancement below. However, unlike the other preset-5 article, this section never satisfies the expected section's model-routing callout (directing inputs to different LLM models based on their strengths) -- no cost-based or capability-based model-routing point appears anywhere in this section. This is a distinct, substantive idea that is fully absent, so CoreContent fails on this gap.

Building a Basic Routing Workflow:
**0:** Both sections implement the identical IntentEnum/UserIntent classification model, the same classify_intent function, the same three specialized prompts, and the same handle_query router. As with every other article graded under this guideline, the expected section's paragraph on intent-classification best practices (taxonomy design, examples for edge cases, a two-stage retrieve-then-classify architecture) has no counterpart, so CoreContent fails on that missing idea cluster. Separately (not scored here -- see the note on this at the top level): this section's code consistently uses an old/incompatible Gemini SDK pattern (genai.GenerativeModel + tools=[PydanticClass] + response.candidates[0].content.parts[0].function_call + PydanticClass.from_dict(), none of which is how either the old or new google-genai SDK actually returns structured output) instead of the expected section's client.models.generate_content(..., config=types.GenerateContentConfig(response_schema=...)) pattern. The conceptual idea (Pydantic-validated structured output) is still present, so this is not counted as a CoreContent gap, but it is flagged prominently below as a new, more severe kind of issue than seen in prior articles.

Orchestrator-Worker Pattern: Dynamic Task Decomposition:
**0:** Both sections define the orchestrator-worker pattern the same way, frame its flexibility/dynamic-nature advantage identically, and walk through the same three-issue customer query with matching schemas (though the workers here are 'pass'-stubbed rather than implemented, unlike the expected section's own aside, which only omits worker internals while showing everything else in full -- the main process_user_query function, unlike in one of the other preset-5 articles, IS shown here). However, per standing ruling, this section never addresses API rate limiting as a real-world limitation of this pattern, despite it dispatching multiple LLM calls per query -- a confirmed omission that fails CoreContent on its own. Separately (not scored here -- see the note on this at the top level): this section's code consistently uses an old/incompatible Gemini SDK pattern (genai.GenerativeModel + tools=[PydanticClass] + response.candidates[0].content.parts[0].function_call + PydanticClass.from_dict(), none of which is how either the old or new google-genai SDK actually returns structured output) instead of the expected section's client.models.generate_content(..., config=types.GenerateContentConfig(response_schema=...)) pattern. The conceptual idea (Pydantic-validated structured output) is still present, so this is not counted as a CoreContent gap, but it is flagged prominently below as a new, more severe kind of issue than seen in prior articles.

Conclusion:
**1:** Both sections recap the same four patterns and close by connecting the lesson to the broader practice of AI engineering and previewing what's next. The next-lesson preview covers the same theme (tools/function calling) without a specific lesson number, which per established precedent is a guideline_adherence matter, not a CoreContent one.
